The global aviation fuel additives market was valued at USD 1.23 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach USD 2.14 billion by 2034, growing at a compound annual growth rate of 6.6%, driven by expanding air traffic and adoption of sustainable aviation fuels.

Regulatory pressure is a key demand driver. In 2024, the International Civil Aviation Organization extended the Clean Sky 2 decarbonisation programme, tightening permissible sulfur and carbon-metal contaminant thresholds by 15%, prompting airlines and fuel suppliers to prioritise additives that ensure cleaner combustion and improved cetane stability.

Advances in organometallic inhibitors and nano-composite slag-preventing agents have extended fuel service life by up to 12%, while higher antioxidant concentration combined with low-sulfur fuels cuts oxidative degradation by 30%, reducing maintenance downtime. Digital analytics platforms matching additive profiles with in-flight performance telemetry via machine learning have reported cost savings of 10-12% compared with conventional grades. Manufacturers spend upwards of 30% of revenue on high-performance testing, while incremental energy savings over legacy products remain near 2%; packaging and distribution bottlenecks add a 5-7% surcharge to fuel costs, and compliance expenditure consumes more than 25% of annual operating expenses at scale.

The market is dominated by BASF with approximately 30% share, followed by Lubrizol, Chevron Oronite with around 15%, Shell Infineum, BP, and TotalEnergies, with boutique players including Innospec, Biobor, Fuels Plus, and regional developers accounting for a growing share. Aviation kerosene fuel is the leading application segment, cleaner additives hold the dominant position by type, and commercial aviation leads among end users, with emerging opportunities concentrated in regional aviation hubs across Southeast Asia, Latin America, and the Middle East.

For 16 years, Mekar has continued to grow in line with the dynamics of the Indonesian economy, from financing to becoming an ecosystem that connects finance, technology, and opportunities in the real sector. text:
In SEA-LNG’s latest report, Liquefaction by Equivalence Pathways for Liquefied Biomethane: A Policy Framework to Enable Scalable Maritime Decarbonisation, SEA-LNG argues that bio-LNG, delivered via mass-balance terminal pathways using liquefaction by equivalence, is the lowest-cost and lowest-emission chain of custody for compliance under FuelEU Maritime and EU ETS.

According to SEA-LNG analysis, bio-LNG bunker volumes grew approximately 100-fold in 2025 compared with 2024, with the overwhelming majority delivered via mass-balance terminal pathway. It can leverage Europe’s existing network of more than 33 LNG import terminals and around 200 000 km of gas transmission infrastructure, without requiring new capital investment in liquefaction plants.

DG ENER is currently preparing proposed revisions to RED Annex V, Annex VI and Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/996, all of which will be binding on Member States and will determine the legal status, GHG accounting treatment and commercial viability of the mass-balance terminal chain of custody. SEA-LNG warns that inadvertent restriction of the pathway through narrow definitions, inflated default emission factors, or inconsistency between the instruments could reduce the availability of compliant low-carbon marine fuel and raise costs for European shipping.

Steve Esau, Chief Operating Officer, SEA-LNG, commented: “The global maritime sector faces a critical decarbonisation challenge with Europe playing an important role in this push. Bio-LNG is one of the few fuels capable of meeting Europe’s maritime decarbonisation obligations at the scale and speed the regulations demand.

“The mass-balance terminal route, using liquefaction by equivalence, is why bio-LNG bunkering grew a hundredfold last year. It uses infrastructure that already exists, so it is scalable and lower cost than the alternatives such as physical segregation. Such dramatic growth illustrates the maritime sector’s appetite for decarbonisation. Europe has an opportunity to become a global leader in bio-methane, e-methane, and renewable methane pathways. Today, DG ENER can unleash Europe’s energy potential.”

SEA-LNG is calling on DG ENER to recognise liquefaction by equivalence and recondenser liquefaction as valid RED III mass-balance pathways, and to as-sign realistic, differentiated default GHG emission values for each liquefaction route based on measured operational data. The coalition is also urging full regulatory coherence between Annexes V/VI and Implementing Regulation 996, to eliminate definitional inconsistency, alongside preservation of cross-border mass-balance mechanisms, including cross-terminal nominations, consistent with single market principles.

Underpinning all of this, SEA-LNG wants long-term investment certainty through a stable regulatory framework extending beyond 2030. Shipowners and operators will look to commit capital for 20 – 25-year vessel lives. Any regulatory instability will delay orders and could lead to reflagging to non-EU jurisdictions.

Mass balance is not a novel concept for the maritime sector: it is already the established chain of custody model for bio-based chemicals and plastics, agricultural commodities such as cotton, and sustainable aviation fuel under both CORSIA and ReFuelEU Aviation.

text:
OMV Petrom has handed Simtel Team an engineering, procurement and construction contract for a battery energy storage system at its Ișalnița solar park in Romania's Dolj county, a deal worth EUR 6.6 million excluding VAT. The installation is slated to deliver 20 megawatts of power and 40 megawatt-hours of capacity, with completion targeted roughly seven months after signing. It marks the first large photovoltaic project to sit entirely under OMV Petrom's ownership.

The solar farm itself carries about 89 megawatts-peak of installed capacity and is expected to generate some 130 gigawatt-hours of electricity annually. Franck Neel, the OMV Petrom board member overseeing gas and energy, framed the investment as a way to sharpen grid flexibility and smooth the integration of renewables into the system.

A Broader Clean-Energy Push Takes Shape

Ișalnița slots into a widening series of commitments through which the group is expanding its clean-power portfolio. OMV Petrom already runs the 860-megawatt Brazi gas-fired plant and says it has more than 1,200 megawatts of renewable capacity under construction. In Bulgaria, a further battery storage system of roughly 600 megawatt-hours is being added at the Gabare site.

Alongside those efforts, the company recently channeled about EUR 115 million into modernizing the electrical infrastructure at its Petrobrazi refinery. The package covers a direct high-voltage link to the transmission grid and a new transformer station, while a 7-megawatt photovoltaic array is going up on the same site. Longer term, the group is also laying plans for sustainable aviation fuel and green hydrogen.

Crude's Climb Sets the Tone

These investments are unfolding against a backdrop in which oil prices are buttressing earnings across the industry. Brent crude traded near USD 108 a barrel on Friday, its highest level since May, after tensions between the United States and Iran disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The rally has been fueled by attacks on maritime routes in the region and by the Houthi militia's capture of the Yemeni port city of Mokha, giving it control of access to the Bab al-Mandab strait. Satellite data also pointed to fires at several points along Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, allegedly caused by Houthi strikes — though confirmation is still pending.

Banks have been revising their forecasts accordingly. HSBC lifted its 2027 Brent projection by USD 20 to USD 85, while Goldman Sachs models USD 80 in its base case for 2027 and flags a worst-case scenario of USD 120. Bank of America sees scope for prices as high as USD 150. For an integrated oil and gas player like OMV, a sustained crude price at these levels translates into stronger upstream revenue — though it also invites political headwinds, with Germany's Left party already calling for a windfall tax amid the jump at the pump.

Record Territory Meets a Skeptical Voice

OMV shares touched an all-time high of EUR 71.45 on Thursday, and at a current price of EUR 70.50 the stock sits just 1.3 percent below that peak. Over twelve months the equity has added roughly 53 percent, with a gain of 51 percent since the start of the year. It trades well above its 200-day moving average of EUR 57.81 — a spread of 22 percent that underscores how far the stock has traveled from its October 2025 low of EUR 42.90.

Even so, Goldman Sachs is sticking with its sell recommendation on the Austrian energy group, albeit while raising its price target from EUR 55 to EUR 60. The bank's caution looks counterintuitive against the fundamentals: OMV changes hands at a price-to-earnings ratio of about 8 and offers a dividend yield above 6 percent. In the second quarter the group comfortably beat expectations, with CCS earnings climbing 65 percent to EUR 1.71 billion against analyst forecasts of EUR 1.66 billion. Net income reached EUR 929 million, ahead of the EUR 820 million consensus. Goldman appears to view the positive news flow as already reflected in the share price — the higher target suggests it acknowledges the fundamental improvement, yet still considers the current valuation premium too rich.

Two Narratives, One Stock

For investors, the Romanian storage contract ties together two threads. On one side, OMV continues to draw support from elevated crude prices that drive its operating results. On the other, the group is methodically building a second pillar through its OMV Petrom subsidiary — solar parks, battery storage and, eventually, green hydrogen. How long the rally holds at these levels will hinge largely on the duration of supply disruptions in the Middle East, and on whether the overvaluation Goldman posits eventually shows up as a correction once conditions in the Gulf settle.

text:
Caramuru Alimentos, owner of the Sinhá brand and a traditional producer of non-GMO soybean meal and derivatives, has been diversifying its revenue sources while waiting for favorable conditions for an initial public offering (IPO), which has long been in the works. The idea remains an option for raising funds for future investments, CEO Marcus Thieme told Valor.

Initial Proagro funding sees first cut since 2018

Corteva and Globalchem announce joint venture

Soybean sowing begins amid rising costs and looming El Niño

In addition to diversifying, the company is expanding in areas where it already operates. As part of this effort, it plans to invest R$100 million in a new warehouse for 60,000 tonnes of sunflower—adding to another warehouse of the same size nearing completion in Silvânia (Goiás)—as well as in new equipment for its plant in Itumbiara (Goiás). This will allow it to increase processing capacity for sunflower oil and derivatives from 100,000 tonnes to 125,000 tonnes per year.

The investment is awaiting approval for state financing lines, as well as approval from the company’s board of directors, but efforts to encourage producers are already underway, according to Thieme.

On Thursday (10), the company held its annual event in Itumbiara with its more than 200 sunflower suppliers in the state. It is no exaggeration to say that Caramuru is the driving force behind sunflower cultivation in Goiás, purchasing around 50,000 tonnes of sunflowers this year from 55,700 hectares, or 88% of the total area planted with the crop in Goiás.

As a result, it is expected to produce around 30,000 tonnes of sunflower oil in 2026, about 30% of the 100,000 tonnes consumed in Brazil. With a goal of expanding the planted area in Goiás to 85,000 hectares by 2028 and producing 47,000 liters of oil following the investments, the company expects to capture a share closer to 50% of Brazil’s retail sunflower oil market with the Sinhá brand. Most of the product currently comes from Argentina, said Tulio Dias, the company’s sunflower business manager.

According to him, one factor supporting the project is the increased availability of sunflower cultivars. There are now 16, three times as many as five harvests ago. High-technology sunflower varieties also cost about half as much as medium-technology corn varieties and can generate three times the profit. In addition, sunflower requires less moisture than corn, a welcome characteristic even in El Niño years, when the weather is drier in the Brazilian Central-West. “We generate demand and structure the supply chain,” Dias said.

An even larger project, which could receive the green light by year-end following an expected financing approval from the Brazilian Development Bank (BNDES) through the Climate Fund, according to Thieme, is the corn ethanol plant in Nova Ubiratã (Mato Grosso).

With an estimated investment of R$1.4 billion, the plant is expected to have capacity to process just under 600,000 tonnes of corn in its first phase, with the possibility of doubling or even tripling that capacity. “It will depend on demand. There is still a lot of room to increase consumption of hydrous ethanol, looking only at the economic factor, as well as other routes to explore, not only SAF [sustainable aviation fuel] but also fuel for maritime shipping,” he said.

A traditional producer and exporter of non-GMO concentrated soy protein (CSP), sold mainly as salmon feed in Scandinavia, Caramuru has also been seeking to tap the market for CSP made from genetically modified soybeans, used in salmon feed.

The company already exports the product to Chile, Turkey, and Southeast Asia. This year, it is expected to sell around 60,000 tonnes of the product and 90,000 tonnes next year, equivalent to the full capacity of the Itumbiara plant. “We are researching new applications, for pigs and shrimp,” he said.

According to Marcus Thieme, Caramuru’s IPO, which has been planned for more than five years, has not been ruled out and remains dependent on better conditions for the transaction—lower interest rates, renewed investor interest, stronger results from agribusiness companies and greater investor understanding of the sector.

The changes the company made in management and corporate governance, initially with the IPO in mind, allowed Caramuru to raise funds through four Agribusiness Receivables Certificates (CRA), which financed investments in recent years, according to Thieme.

The executive does not rule out an IPO next year, depending on the macroeconomic environment. “In the past, we used to talk about an IPO window. Now we talk about a crack,” he said. “There could indeed be room for equity if there is a clearer signal of more attractive interest rates. As interest rates fall, equity offerings become more competitive.”

For Caramuru, Brazil’s 10th-largest biodiesel producer, a signal regarding the adoption of higher biodiesel blending percentages in diesel will also be crucial for investment decisions. The government is still conducting technical studies to implement B16 (16% biodiesel), something that had been expected at the beginning of the year.

Under the agreement, GS Caltex will supply SAF over the next year to DHL Express aircraft refuelling in Korea.
GS Caltex said it plans to expand SAF production and supply to airlines as demand for the fuel increases.
“Through the SAF supply agreement with DHL Express, we have taken another step toward expanding our SAF customers,” a GS Caltex spokesperson said, adding that the company will continue to expand its SAF and broader biofuel businesses in response to market demand.

text:
South Korean energy company GS Caltex will supply sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) to global logistics company DHL Express, expanding its presence in the growing SAF market, biofuels international reported.

The two companies signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on September 8 at GS Tower in Gangnam, Seoul, to establish a partnership aimed at reducing carbon emissions through the use of sustainable aviation fuel.

Under the agreement, GS Caltex will supply SAF over the next year to DHL Express aircraft refuelling in Korea. The contracted volume is equivalent to 2,000 tonnes of neat SAF, or 100% SAF.

The SAF supplied by GS Caltex is produced through a co-processing method and has received ISCC EU certification in accordance with the European Union’s Renewable Energy Directive.

GS Caltex said it plans to expand SAF production and supply to airlines as demand for the fuel increases.

“Through the SAF supply agreement with DHL Express, we have taken another step toward expanding our SAF customers,” a GS Caltex spokesperson said, adding that the company will continue to expand its SAF and broader biofuel businesses in response to market demand.

The company has continued to produce and supply SAF in line with developments in the global fuel market and changes in government policies.

The company’s business model is built around:

Producing renewable diesel and renewable fuels.

Developing renewable hydrogen capabilities.

Advancing sustainable aviation fuel opportunities.

Participating in low-carbon fuel Credit markets.

Leveraging existing energy infrastructure for renewable applications.

The company generates value by converting renewable feedstocks into cleaner fuel alternatives that can support transportation and industrial decarbonisation efforts.

Tidewater Renewables’ strategy combines traditional energy infrastructure expertise with renewable fuel production capabilities. This approach allows the company to participate in the energy transition while utilising established operational knowledge.

The company’s growth depends on production efficiency, regulatory support, renewable fuel demand and successful execution of expansion projects.

title: Issue 211: Singapore defers green jet fuel levy for cargo; TUV SUD opens decarbonisation centre

The sector is veering further in the wrong direction with regards to sustainable aviation fuel, and it seems increasingly likely that the industry will have to adopt more realistic targets or accept widespread non-compliance.

text:
Energy transition

Sustainable aviation fuel needs a reality check

Singapore’s decision to delay a green jet fuel levy for air cargo is the latest challenge confronting efforts to decarbonise the aviation sector.

The sector is veering further in the wrong direction with regards to sustainable aviation fuel, and it seems increasingly likely that the industry will have to adopt more realistic targets or accept widespread non-compliance. If that happens, investors in the sector may face higher-for-longer emissions in their portfolios as well as greater uncertainty about climate transition risks.
